desc:
The string expr is an arithmetic expression without spaces and without brackets. It contains non-negative integer literals and the binary operators +, -, * and /. Multiplication and division have higher priority than addition and subtraction, and operators of the same priority are applied from left to right. Division is integer division that drops the fractional part.

Evaluate the expression and return its value. Do not use any built-in function that evaluates a string as code.

Examples: 3+2*2 is 7, 14-3/2 is 13, 100/10/5 is 2 and 5-6/4 is 4.
constraints: expr contains only digits and the characters '+', '-', '*', '/' and is a valid expression (it starts and ends with a digit, no two operators are adjacent)
Literals have no leading zeros (except the single digit "0") and are at most 2<sup>31</sup> - 1
Never divides by zero; every literal, every partial product or quotient and every partial sum has absolute value at most 2<sup>31</sup> - 1
hints: Without brackets there is only one level of priority to handle: products and quotients bind tighter than sums and differences.
Treat the expression as a sum of signed terms. A term is a chain of numbers joined by * and /. Keep a stack (or just a running total and the last term) of the terms.

Remember the operator that came before the number you just finished reading. +: push the number. -: push its negative. * or /: combine it with the top of the stack. At the end add up the stack. Add a sentinel operator at the end so the last number is processed too.
editorial: Split the expression into terms separated by + and -. Inside a term the operators * and / are applied from left to right, and the value of the whole expression is the sum of the signed terms. A stack of term values handles this naturally.

Read the string left to right, collecting the digits of the current number. When you hit an operator (or the end of the string) the number is complete, and you act according to the previous operator: + pushes num, - pushes -num, * replaces the top by top * num, / replaces it by top / num rounded toward zero. Then remember the new operator and reset the number.

The top of the stack can be negative (the term was subtracted), so round toward zero: dividing -6 by 4 must give -1, which is the same as -(6 / 4). Finally return the sum of the stack. Time O(n); space O(n) with a stack, or O(1) if you only keep the running total and the last term.
